name: British

attributes.attribute: the oldest attested stage of Celtic speech in Britain
a P-Celtic language family of Britain and Brittany
the Brythonic-speaking natives of Britain and their heirs

sources: Jackson, Kenneth. Language and History in Early Britain. Edinburgh University Press, 1953.
text: British names the ancient Celtic speech of Britain. In Celtic studies it is the oldest attested stage of Brythonic. The language survives in proper names from Caesar's raids in 55 and 54 BC. This form kept its Proto-Celtic final syllables longer than later speech. Jackson in 1953 called this stage Late British. Held in Jackson, that phase ran from the mid-fifth to the mid-sixth century. It ended when those syllables faded and fell away. The term once meant the pre-English folk of Britain and their Welsh, Cornish, and Breton heirs. By the mid-1800s it had stopped meaning Welsh. The later sense of British instead covered all island speech and imperial rule.

okr.objective: Portray British as the ancient Brythonic tongue of Britain and the source of later Welsh forms.
key_results: British is the oldest attested Celtic stage of Britain.
Jackson assigned the Late British phase to the mid-5th to mid-6th century.
The older sense named the pre-English people and their heirs.
By the mid-1800s the term had ceased to mean Welsh.
